measures.t: A RESOLUTION to propose an amendment to Article I, Section 15 of the Constitution of Tennessee, relative to bail.
measures.s: This amendment changes Article I, section 15 of the Tennessee Constitution by allowing a court to hold a defendant without bail before trial when that defendant is accused of: an offense punishable by the death penalty, an act of terrorism, second degree murder, aggravated rape of a child, aggravated rape, grave torture, or any crime for which a convicted person would be required to serve eighty-five percent of their sentence. This amendment requires courts to state on the record the reasons for their decision to grant or deny bail in those cases.
measures.sb: printed on the ballot as the amendment's summary, above the question
measures.f:
LOCAL GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES Mandatory FY26-27 $9,400
The one-time increase in local expenditures in FY26-27 for publishing costs is estimated to be $9,400 based upon the cost of recent publications incurred by the Secretary of State.
measures.fb: The Tennessee General Assembly's Fiscal Review Committee, in its fiscal note dated January 18, 2025 (the estimated cost to counties of publishing the longer sample ballot). It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment needs more YES votes than NO votes, and its YES votes must also be more than half of all the votes cast for governor in the same election. A voter does not have to vote for governor to vote on the amendment. (Tennessee Constitution, article XI, section 3)
measures.h: Proposed by the General Assembly in two steps, as article XI, section 3 of the Tennessee Constitution requires: first passed by a majority of each house in Senate Joint Resolution 919 of the 113th General Assembly, then passed again by two thirds of each house of the 114th General Assembly as Senate Joint Resolution 25 (the House concurred on April 21, 2025). It goes to the voters at the next election in which a governor is chosen.
measures.nt: The title shown is the resolution's own caption; the ballot prints the amendment as "Constitutional Amendment #1", then its summary, then the question, which carries the words to be deleted and the words to be put in their place. The number, summary and question are from the Hamilton County Election Commission's official sample ballot and are the same, word for word, on the Davidson County Election Commission's sample ballot (the Secretary of State's page could not be read here). A line break in the middle of a sentence on the sample ballot is not kept. The fiscal note is the General Assembly's and is not printed on the ballot.

measures.t: A RESOLUTION to propose an amendment to Article II, Section 28 of the Constitution of Tennessee, to prohibit taxation of property by the State.
measures.q:
Shall Article II, Section 28 of the Constitution of the State of Tennessee be amended by deleting the following language from the first sentence:
In accordance with the following provisions, all property real, personal or mixed shall be subject to taxation, but the Legislature
and substituting instead the following:
In accordance with the following provisions, all property real, personal, or mixed shall be subject to taxation, but the Legislature shall not levy, authorize, or otherwise permit any state tax upon such property, and the Legislature

measures.t: A RESOLUTION proposing an amendment to Article I, Section 35 of the Constitution of Tennessee, relative to the rights of crime victims.
measures.s: This amendment changes Article I, section 35 of the Tennessee Constitution by clarifying existing rights for crime victims and adding new rights. The amendment gives victims new rights: to fair treatment; to be informed about and participate in the parole process; to be protected from harassment, intimidation, and abuse; to be informed of the minimum sentence the convicted criminal will serve, as well as their scheduled release date; and to have their safety, their family's safety, and the public's safety taken into account before any decision is made to release the convicted criminal. The amendment also maintains or clarifies victims' existing rights: to be informed about legal proceedings involving the accused or convicted criminal; to be present at public criminal proceedings; to be informed of any release, transfer, or escape of the accused or convicted criminal; to talk to prosecutors; to make statements about conviction, sentencing, or release of the accused person; to a speedy resolution of the case; to restitution from the convicted criminal; and to be informed of their rights. The amendment does not restrict the powers of prosecutors or courts and does not create a cause of action or claim for damages against the State of Tennessee.

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the Tennessee's election office’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The November list is not loaded yet. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local races are not loaded for Tennessee yet; they are loaded for 39 states so far, shown on the states page.
lists

What is read. From those lists this site reads only the office, the district, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one. Addresses, phone numbers, e-mail and websites, where a list carries them, are never read, kept or shown. No photos, ages, biographies or campaign money are shown for state candidates.
lists
Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page and nothing more.
maps

Maps and “use my location”. District lines are the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary files), the lines the state pages draw; your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your district. Your location is worked out on your own device and never sent anywhere; a rounded copy (about half a mile) is kept on the device, with your choices, until you tap “Forget”. A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are counted only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Published polls by other pollsters that we have checked against their own release are shown apart, under Other published polls, for reference, and are never counted in the average; the rest are counted and named. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found by your own pick: the state’s congressional lines changed for 2026, so a location cannot place you in a district here.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Past results: Wisconsin, Minnesota's local races, and every precinct
items: Wisconsin's past results are here: Congress, the Legislature, district attorneys, statewide questions, and Milwaukee and Dane counties' own offices and questions, from the state Elections Commission's official files.

Minnesota now has every local contest of 2020, 2022 and 2024: judges, county offices, cities, townships, school boards, soil and water and hospital districts, and local questions, read from the Secretary of State's own result files (as kept by the Internet Archive after the count was certified) and checked precinct by precinct against the certified results.
Precinct by precinct: on the Past results page, open any county's or contest's precinct table to see each precinct's figures, for the 44 states that publish them. They load only when you open them.

changelog.title: Past results for every state, and the ballot in Spanish (a draft)
items: Past results now cover 49 states and the District of Columbia: the November general elections of 2020, 2022 and 2024, from President down to county offices, cities, townships, school boards, special districts and ballot questions wherever the state or county publishes official figures. Wisconsin's official files are not reachable yet, and the page says so.

Figures are shown by county and by city or town. Where a state's figures come from a compilation rather than its own official count, they are labelled secondary and no winner is marked from them. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.
Each race page's "This seat before" now finds past elections in every loaded state.

On the draft site only: the ballot pages, menus, Help and the reading settings can be read in Spanish ("¿Leer en español?"). Each translated page says it was translated by Claude, an AI model, and not yet reviewed by a person. Names, office titles as printed and the words on your ballot stay in English; office titles show a Spanish translation beside the official English.
Ballot pages now say in one plain sentence what each office does, at the Beginner and Easy levels, with the official sources one tap away.

changelog.title: Past results: how places and seats voted in 2020, 2022 and 2024
items: New in Election Night: "Past results". Pick a state and a year (the November general elections of 2024, 2022 and 2020), then any contest on that ballot: names and parties as printed, votes and shares, the certified total and where it comes from, a county map, and the figures for each county, city or township.

North Dakota and Iowa are here in full, down to county offices, townships, soil and water districts and every ballot question. Illinois has Congress, the Legislature, judges and the statewide questions; Minnesota has President, Congress, the Legislature, Governor and the statewide offices. Their county and local races are next, and the page says which parts are still missing.

On The Ballot: race pages now have "This seat before", the same seat's past elections, with a note when the district's lines were different then. Ballot question pages have "Questions voters here decided before".
Every figure comes from the state's or county's official certified count and was checked against the official totals. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.

changelog.title: The dashboard
items: New: a dashboard of the whole record, in three views. "Your place at a glance" shows any state or the whole country: what is on its ballot, who holds its seats, its ballot questions, and a link to its mail-voting facts. "The record, filtered" turns Congress's bills and floor votes into a sentence and charts you can narrow by chamber, topic and year. "Every state, side by side" puts all the states on one map, one measure at a time, with a two-state comparison.

Every figure is counted from the site's records when the page is built, and every chart says where its numbers come from and what they cannot tell you. Places can be compared; people are never ranked.
Beginner shows a few plain tiles; Medium adds the charts; Advanced opens the sources. Each view has its own address and a Share button.
The dashboard is linked from the home page, the menus, the On The Ballot door and Help.

changelog.title: Vote by mail, and questions answered
items: Every state's ballot page now has "Vote by mail or absentee": the last day to ask for a mail ballot and the last day to send it back for November 3, how to ask (the state's own link), how to send it back, what the envelope needs, how to track it, early voting in person, and what the state says for students at school elsewhere in the state or in another state, and for military and overseas voters. Every fact links to the state's own page or law and shows when it was checked. When a deadline has passed, the page says so and points to voting early or on Election Day.
"Your ballot" now says, under the election date, when to ask for a mail ballot.
The Congress ballot pages link each state to its mail-voting facts.

New: On The Ballot's questions page, with plain answers on voting by mail, students, military and overseas voters, moving, checking your registration, finding your polling place, when polls close, early voting, ID, tracking your ballot and a spoiled or lost ballot. Pick your state and each answer uses its own rules.
Every fact comes from the state's own election office or law, or from federal voting sites, and a second check re-read each source. The state election office always has the final word.

changelog.title: Share anything
items: Every part of the site now has a Share button: pages, races, ballot questions, counties, members, bills, votes, maps, the district lenses and Election Night. On a phone it opens your phone's own share sheet. On a computer it offers Copy link, e-mail, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Bluesky, WhatsApp and Reddit (and text messages on a phone).
Nothing is sent until you pick a place. The place you pick then sees the link. No sharing buttons from those companies are loaded on these pages.
Every race, ballot question and county, down to the local contests, now has its own preview picture, so a shared link shows what it is about.
"Share my ballot" shares your precinct's ballot, after a note saying the link shows roughly where you vote. A shared link never carries your exact location.
The ready-made message sticks to the facts, for example: "U.S. Senate, Minnesota: who is on the November 3 ballot, from the official list."

polls.note: The Beacon Center's marginals give an independent candidate 7% and undecided 4% among likely voters. Among all registered voters who answered (1,149), Blackburn had 46%, Green 33%, an independent candidate 8% and 14% were undecided.

news.note: Registered voters who said they were almost certain to vote or would probably vote. TargetSmart designed and administered the survey (its methodology page): 300 by live phone from its voter file, 300 online by an email or text link. Shares include voters leaning to a candidate; Hatley and Pinkston are independents; the rest is undecided (other candidate 0). The toplines name no sponsor. A Tennessee Lookout column of September 25 quotes Lauren Pinkston calling it a poll funded by a PAC supporting Green; Wikipedia (secondary) lists the Progress Fund. Neither is the release.
